question: Rewrite the clinical guidance on ALL into a public health advisory for families with children and adolescents, emphasizing early symptoms, risk factors, and the importance of prompt diagnosis and specialized care.
pred_answer:
Public Health Advisory: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) in Children and Adolescents

ALL is the most common cancer diagnosed in children. It is a fast-growing blood cancer that starts in disease-fighting white blood cells called lymphocytes. Families should be aware that accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat ALL, and that treatment depends on the type of ALL, age at diagnosis, and other factors.

Risk factors are things that increase the chance of developing a disease; known risk factors are listed in the ALL guide. Prompt diagnosis matters: in general, ALL is diagnosed when 20 percent or more lymphoblasts are present in the bone marrow, meaning at least 1 out of every 5 bone marrow cells are lymphoblasts, although in certain cases diagnosis is possible with less than 20 percent lymphoblasts. Blood and bone marrow tests and imaging studies are used to determine the treatment plan, and treatment is based on the findings of these tests.

Families should seek care at an experienced children’s (pediatric) leukemia center and consider seeking the opinion of an ALL specialist. The ALL guide covers treatment for infants, children, and young adults. Pediatric refers to ALL found in infants, children, and young adults, including anyone 18 years of age or under and certain adolescents and young adults (AYAs). An AYA is someone 15 to 39 years of age at initial cancer diagnosis. AYAs may be treated at pediatric or adult centers depending on the type of cancer; this book applies to AYAs being treated at a pediatric or children’s cancer center. Infant ALL treatment is different than for other age groups.

Families have an important role to play in their child’s care. Many people feel more satisfied when they play an active role in their care, and you are more likely to get the care you want by asking questions and making shared decisions with your care team. Advocate for your child and yourself. With better understanding, you will be more prepared to discuss care with your child’s team and share your concerns. You may not know what to ask your care team; that’s common. Each chapter in the ALL guide ends with a “Questions to ask” section to help you get more information on all aspects of care.

Chapter 2 of the ALL guide, “Testing for ALL,” covers general health tests, blood tests, fertility (all genders), preventing pregnancy, tissue tests, genetic risk testing, genetic and biomarker testing, imaging tests, lumbar puncture, heart tests, bone marrow tests, B-ALL risk groups, pharmacogenomic testing, key points, and questions to ask. It also addresses how fertility might be impacted by treatment. More information on fertility and family planning is available in the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer. Chapter 9: Other resources provides information on patient advocacy groups and where to get help. More information for those seeking ALL treatment at an adult cancer center can be found in the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.

question: Imagine you are a medical oncologist receiving a new patient diagnosed with Stage II pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Construct an initial management plan including diagnostic confirmation, staging, treatment options, risk assessment, and multidisciplinary coordination, based strictly on the clinical practice guideline.
pred_answer: Initial management should include diagnostic confirmation through testing when PDAC is suspected, staging based on tumor size and extent/lymph node spread, multidisciplinary team coordination, assessment of resectability and surgical candidacy by the team, consideration of drug treatment and other nonsurgical options, hereditary and risk-factor assessment, and discussion of clinical trials, with care planning individualized because there is no single best treatment and treatment is not planned mainly by the five stages.
raw_response:
The clinical practice guideline states that staging, treatment planning, and multidisciplinary care for PDAC are based on the provided facts, not on a single stage-based algorithm. Diagnostic confirmation is prompted by suspicion and testing (F28–F29), while staging is based on tumor size and spread, including lymph node involvement (F6, F18). Stage II PDAC may be resectable, as some stage 1–3 patients undergo surgery (F15), but there is no single best treatment and initial treatment is not planned mainly by stage (F16). Surgery is not best for most patients (F22); drug treatment is often used to control growth and reduce symptoms (F23). pred_answer:
Public Health Advisory: Know the Risks of Pancreatic Cancer

Pancreatic cancer begins in the pancreas and includes two main types: exocrine and endocrine tumors. While experts do not know the exact cause, several risk factors are known.

Risk factors include diabetes, chronic inflammation of the pancreas, smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, a less healthy diet, and exposure to cancer-causing chemicals such as pesticides. Some risk is hereditary: conditions such as familial malignant melanoma syndrome, hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome, hereditary pancreatitis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome can increase risk. Having close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma is also a risk factor.

Possible signs may include wider-than-normal pancreatic ducts or an inflamed pancreas seen on x-rays. Because pancreatic cancer is often challenging to treat, knowing your risk and seeking early evaluation are important. A risk assessment can help determine whether further testing or treatment is needed. If you have risk factors or concerning symptoms, talk with your care team promptly. Early diagnosis and timely risk assessment can guide the best course of action.

question: Rewrite the key points from the prostate cancer guideline as a public health advisory aimed at men over 50, emphasizing risk factors, early detection, and available treatments.
pred_answer:
**Public Health Advisory: Prostate Cancer Awareness for Men Over 50**

**Know Your Risk**
- Age is the biggest risk factor: prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in men aged 65 and above.
- Having a close family member (parent or sibling) with prostate cancer increases your chance of getting it.
- All men with a prostate are at risk—prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in American males after skin cancer.
- Other factors may also increase risk; talk to your doctor about your personal risk profile.

**Early Detection Saves Lives**
- Most men with early-stage prostate cancer have no symptoms—you don’t have to feel sick to have cancer.
- When found early, prostate cancer has one of the highest survival rates of any cancer.
- An unusually high PSA level in the blood may be a sign of prostate cancer.
- Testing begins with screening (such as PSA), followed by general health tests and, if needed, diagnostic tests like biopsy—the most reliable way to confirm cancer.
- Early detection and treatment can greatly reduce the chances of developing advanced-stage prostate cancer.
- Not all early-stage cases require immediate treatment; some can be monitored safely.

**Treatment Options Are Available**
- Prostate cancer is a complex disease with many treatment options.
- Treatments for advanced-stage cancer include hormone therapy and non-hormone therapies such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation.
- Combining therapies can be more effective than using a single therapy alone; hormone therapy is often combined with other treatments.
- Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) lowers testosterone to very low levels, which can shrink tumors or slow their growth.
- Orchiectomy (surgical removal of the testicles) is an option but is much less common today because reversible hormone therapy is available.
- Your care team will develop a personalized treatment plan based on your test results and risk assessment.

**Take Action**
If you are over 50, talk to your healthcare provider about prostate cancer screening and risk assessment. Early detection and informed treatment decisions can make a significant difference.

question: You are a medical intern on the oncology service. Write a SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) progress note for a patient with high-risk localized prostate cancer, integrating clinical presentation, diagnostic findings, risk stratification, and next steps based on the guideline.
pred_answer:
**SOAP Progress Note – High-Risk Localized Prostate Cancer**

**Subjective:**
Patient is a [age] year-old male presenting for follow-up after recent prostate cancer diagnosis. He reports [e.g., urinary symptoms, no bone pain, weight stable]. He has reviewed his test results with the care team and asks, “How soon can I start treatment to get rid of it?” He expresses interest in a second opinion and has brought his spouse to the visit to listen and take notes.

**Objective:**
- PSA: [e.g., 25 ng/mL] (high; elevated PSA may indicate prostate cancer and higher disease burden).
- Digital rectal exam: [e.g., firm nodule, cT2b].
- Biopsy: [e.g., 12 cores, 6 positive, Gleason 4+4=8, Grade Group 4]. Pathologist confirmed prostate cancer.
- Molecular biomarker testing on biopsy sample: [e.g., Decipher high-risk].
- Imaging: [e.g., MRI prostate shows extracapsular extension? PSMA PET/CT: no metastatic disease]. Tumor stage: cT2c N0 M0.
- Risk group calculation: PSA, Grade Group, tumor stage, and biopsy results combined → **high-risk localized prostate cancer** (e.g., NCCN high-risk: PSA >20, Grade Group 4-5, or cT3a).

**Assessment:**
High-risk localized prostate cancer. Risk stratification: high risk for recurrence and progression. Prognosis is guarded compared to lower-risk groups; patients with higher risk usually require more aggressive treatment. Risk assessment considers likelihood of recurrence and whether it can be controlled with different treatment. Molecular biomarker test flags higher risk, which may give a head start on treatment. No evidence of metastasis on imaging, so disease is localized but high-risk.

**Plan:**
1. **Multidisciplinary discussion:** Case reviewed at tumor board; discussion between cancer doctors recommended.
2. **Second opinion:** Refer to specialty center for second opinion, as recommended if possible.
3. **Treatment planning:** After all tests, discuss results and develop individualized plan. For high-risk disease, more aggressive treatment is indicated. Options include radical prostatectomy with possible adjuvant therapy, or external beam radiation therapy with androgen deprivation therapy (e.g., 18–24 months). Consider molecular biomarker test results to refine risk.
4. **Additional testing:** If not already done, consider molecular biomarker testing on biopsy sample to assess lower vs. higher risk. Imaging may be repeated as clinically indicated; not all tests are needed for every patient.
5. **Monitoring:** Baseline labs, bone health assessment, and PSA monitoring. Tests will be used to monitor treatment response and health after treatment ends.
6. **Patient education:** Discuss prognosis, risk of recurrence, and treatment options. Provide NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Early-Stage Prostate Cancer resource. Encourage bringing someone to testing and asking questions.
7. **Follow-up:** Return in [e.g., 2–4 weeks] to finalize treatment decision after second opinion and multidisciplinary review.

question: Imagine you are an endocrinologist receiving a referral for a 45-year-old patient with an incidentally discovered adrenal mass on CT scan. Draft a detailed diagnostic workup plan, integrating risk assessment for malignancy and hormone excess, as recommended by the guidelines.
pred_answer:
Diagnostic workup plan:
1. Confirm incidental finding on CT; note size, imaging features (F9, F10).
2. Biochemical testing for hormone excess: measure cortisol, aldosterone, DHEA, and medullary hormones (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine) in blood, urine, and/or saliva (F8, F30, F37). Test for Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess) and aldosteronoma (aldosterone excess) (F29, F48).
3. Assess symptoms: hormonal changes such as excess facial hair, hair loss, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, shrinking testicles (F40); symptoms from excess hormones (F51).
4. Risk assessment for malignancy: most tumors benign (F3, F22); malignant rare (F12). ACC rare but most common adrenal cancer (F11), peaks in 40s–50s (F23). Consider FDG-PET: benign tumors often not bright (F43). If functional, may produce multiple hormones (F44).
5. Diagnosis based on test results (F33); testing determines treatment plan (F7, F49, F50). If cancer spread beyond adrenal glands, cure less likely; treatment delays progression (F31, F46).
6. Multidisciplinary care team may include endocrinologist, radiologist, surgeon, etc. (F36).

The patient has an incidentally discovered adrenal mass, which is often asymptomatic and found through imaging (F9, F10). Testing includes measuring hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva (F8), and should be prompted by any hormone-related symptoms (F5, F51). For risk assessment of malignancy, consider that most adrenal tumors are benign (F3, F22), but malignant tumors are rare (F12). ACC is the most common adrenal cancer but very rare (F11), with incidence peaking in adults in their 40s and 50s (F23). If the tumor is functional, it may produce more than one hormone (F44). Imaging characteristics such as FDG-PET avidity can help differentiate benign from malignant (F43). Diagnosis is based on test results (F33), and testing is used to diagnose and plan treatment (F7, F49, F50). Care team may include endocrinologist and others (F36). If cancer is suspected, early detection improves curability (F46, F31).

question: Transform the guideline evidence into a structured discharge summary for a patient recently treated for adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), including presentation, diagnostic process, risk assessment, and follow-up recommendations.
pred_answer: Structured discharge summary — Diagnosis: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), a rare malignant adrenal cortex tumor, possibly functioning or nonfunctioning. Diagnostic Process: Biochemical tests (blood, urine, saliva hormones), imaging (CT/MRI, FDG-PET), and genetic testing for hereditary conditions (e.g., Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome). Risk Assessment: Most adrenal tumors are benign; ACC is rare (300–500 diagnoses/year), malignant, and can metastasize (e.g., to bones); cure less likely if spread beyond adrenal glands. Follow-up Recommendations: Monitor for progression/recurrence, especially if spread; treatment may delay progression or recurrence; continue testing-based treatment planning and surveillance.

question: Imagine you are a public health officer tasked with drafting a community advisory about the importance of recognizing symptoms and hereditary risk factors for adrenal tumors. Your advisory should integrate at least five key points from the guidelines.
pred_answer:
Community Advisory: Recognizing Symptoms and Hereditary Risk Factors for Adrenal Tumors

Adrenal tumors are rare, with about 300 to 500 people diagnosed each year. While most adrenal tumors are benign, some can be malignant. Importantly, adrenal tumors often do not cause symptoms and may be found incidentally through imaging tests such as CT or MRI scans performed for another reason. When symptoms do occur, they may include hormonal changes such as excess facial hair, hair loss on the head, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, or shrinking testicles, as well as nonspecific symptoms like weight gain, fever, loss of appetite, muscle weakness, nausea, vomiting, or pink/purple stretch marks. Half of those with adrenal cancer will have symptoms caused by hormones produced by the tumor. In addition to symptoms, certain hereditary conditions can increase the risk of developing an adrenal tumor, though this accounts for only a small portion of cases. These hereditary conditions are mutations passed down from biological parent to child through genes and include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Hereditary paragangliomapheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome. If you have any of these signs, symptoms, or a family history of these hereditary conditions, make sure to discuss them with your health care provider. Testing is used to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. Early recognition and discussion with a provider can lead to timely diagnosis and appropriate care.

question: You are an oncologist preparing a referral letter for a 45-year-old woman recently diagnosed with Stage II, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. Summarize the diagnostic workup, relevant biomarkers, and outline the initial treatment plan for the receiving multidisciplinary team.
pred_answer: Diagnostic workup: biopsy with HR testing (IHC for ER/PR and HER2), biomarker testing, and staging via TNM plus receptor status. Biomarkers: hormone receptor-positive (ER and/or PR positive), HER2-negative. Treatment: endocrine therapy (blocks estrogen/progesterone signaling), possibly combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for HR-positive, HER2-negative disease; no HER2-targeted therapy.
raw_response:
The diagnostic workup for this patient includes a biopsy sample that undergoes hormone receptor (HR) testing, which is recommended for any new tumor (F31, F32). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) measures receptors and can identify estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors in breast cancer cells; a pathologist then measures how many cells have estrogen and/or progesterone receptors and the number of receptors inside each cell (F18, F19, F20). Biomarker testing, which includes HER2 and hormone receptor status, identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment (F9, F10, F12). Staging incorporates ER status, PR status, and HER2 status, along with imaging and other testing, using the TNM system to assign a final numbered stage (F13, F14, F15, F35, F43, F44, F45, F46).

Relevant biomarkers: The tumor is hormone receptor-positive, meaning IHC finds estrogen and/or progesterone hormone receptors (F1). Most breast cancers are hormone receptor-positive, and these tend to grow slower than HR-negative cancers (F2, F3). Estrogen receptor (ER) is stimulated by estrogen and provides survival and proliferation signals, and PR expression also suggests the tumor is estrogen dependent (F8, F26). The cancer is HER2-negative.

Initial treatment plan: Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is treated with endocrine therapy, which blocks estrogen receptor signaling; endocrine therapy blocks estrogen or progesterone to treat hormone receptor-positive breast cancer (F7, F30). For hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative cancer, taking a CDK4/6 inhibitor with endocrine therapy may help control cancer longer (F33). Cancer cells deprived of estrogen or which have their ER signal blocked with treatment may stop growing or die (F25). Since the cancer is HER2-negative, HER2-targeted therapy is not indicated.

Answer: Diagnostic workup: biopsy with HR testing (IHC for ER/PR and HER2), biomarker testing, and staging via TNM plus receptor status. Biomarkers: hormone receptor-positive (ER and/or PR positive), HER2-negative. Treatment: endocrine therapy (blocks estrogen/progesterone signaling), possibly combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for HR-positive, HER2-negative disease; no HER2-targeted therapy.

question: Imagine you are a medical intern tasked with writing a discharge summary for a patient with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) who has completed neoadjuvant systemic therapy and modified radical mastectomy. Structure the summary to include diagnosis, key findings, treatment course, and follow-up recommendations.
pred_answer: Discharge summary: Diagnosis: Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), an aggressive invasive ductal carcinoma with lymph vessel blockage in the breast skin, typically stage 3 or 4 at diagnosis. Key findings: Red, swollen, warm breast with erythema, edema, Peau d'orange, and skin thickening; no palpable lump often; diagnosis confirmed by biopsy and imaging. Treatment course: Completed neoadjuvant systemic therapy followed by modified radical mastectomy; radiation therapy per protocol; treatment similar across genders. Follow-up: Regular monitoring for recurrence and metastasis; seek care for new skin changes; breast specialist referral; surveillance for side effects and overall health.
raw_response:
1. **Diagnosis**: The patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a rare and aggressive form of breast cancer characterized by cancer cells blocking lymph vessels in the skin of the breast, leading to redness, swelling, and warmth. IBC is often difficult to diagnose due to its infection-like presentation and the frequent absence of a palpable lump. Most IBC cases are invasive ductal carcinomas, and at diagnosis, IBC is typically stage 3 or 4 disease.

2. **Key Findings**: Clinical presentation included erythema, edema, and skin changes such as Peau d'orange and skin thickening. Diagnostic confirmation involved imaging, blood tests, and a skin biopsy, as IBC can mimic an infection. Hormone receptor status, HER2 status, and biomarker testing were performed to guide therapy.

3. **Treatment Course**: The patient received neoadjuvant systemic therapy (preoperative systemic treatment) to shrink the tumor, followed by modified radical mastectomy to remove the breast and lymph nodes. Postoperative radiation therapy is planned or has been completed as part of the treatment regimen. Treatment approaches for IBC are similar across genders, though breast cancer occurs more frequently in those assigned female at birth.

4. **Follow-up Recommendations**: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor for recurrence and metastasis, as breast cancer can spread through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. Patients should be advised to seek medical attention for any new or unusual breast skin changes, including redness, swelling, or warmth. Referral to a breast specialist and continued surveillance for treatment-related side effects, including fertility and general health monitoring, are recommended.

question: You are a patient advocate tasked with drafting a public health notice to educate the community about breast cancer risk factors, screening, and the importance of early detection. Your notice should reference clinical evidence and recommended practices.
pred_answer:
**Public Health Notice: Breast Cancer Awareness, Screening, and Early Detection**

Breast cancer can affect anyone, including those assigned male at birth, though it occurs more frequently in persons assigned female at birth. Inside breasts are lobules (milk glands) and ducts, and breast cancer often starts in these structures before spreading into surrounding tissue, at which point it is considered invasive. Not all breast cancers are the same.

**Screening and Early Detection**
The goal of breast cancer screening is to find cancer early, before symptoms start, when treatment is more likely to be successful and can save lives. Regular screening mammograms are recommended for those assigned female at birth when there are no signs or symptoms. Those assigned male at birth do not undergo routine mammogram screening, but if you notice breast pain, redness, or a change in the size or shape of one breast, see your health care provider and ask about recommended tests. Anyone can develop breast cancer, including those assigned male at birth, and treatment is very similar for all genders.

**Risk Factors and Genetic Testing**
Your care team may ask about your family health history. Genetic counseling and testing should be done if you are at risk for hereditary breast cancer.

**Know the Warning Signs**
The speaker was a nurse and didn't know you could have breast cancer without a lump. Seek medical attention right away for strange skin changes to the breast. Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) can happen in those assigned male at birth, so skin changes should not be ignored. Ask for a referral to a breast specialist, if possible.

**Self-Advocacy and Shared Decisions**
You are an important member of your cancer care team. Patients are advised to advocate for themselves in their cancer care. To get the best care, you should advocate for yourself. You have an important role to play in your care. You're more likely to get the care you want by asking questions and making shared decisions with your care team. It is important to understand what you are going through. If your doctor says something you do not understand, let them know. Many people feel more satisfied when they play an active role in their care.

**Additional Cancer Screening**
Get screened for other types of cancer, such as breast, cervical, colorectal, or prostate cancer, as recommended by your health care provider.

pred_answer:
SOAP Progress Note – Metastatic Breast Cancer Follow-Up

Subjective:
- Patient with history of breast cancer, now diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer (MBC), also called advanced breast cancer.
- Reports possible symptoms related to distant spread; MBC has spread outside the breast and underarm lymph nodes to distant parts of the body.
- May have bone pain, respiratory symptoms, or other site-specific complaints depending on metastasis to bone, lung, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes.
- Denies or reports axillary lymph node involvement; note that MBC can occur even when axillary lymph nodes do not have cancer.

Objective:
- TNM staging: M1 indicates distant metastasis is found; M0 means no evidence of distant metastasis.
- Documented distant metastasis confirmed, consistent with stage 4/metastatic disease.
- Imaging/pathology may show metastasis in bone (including spine), lung, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes; M1a = lung metastasis, M1b = bone or other distant sites.
- Biomarker testing performed or planned to identify targetable features of the cancer.
- Breast cancer that has metastasized retains the name breast cancer despite spread to other parts of the body.

Assessment:
- Metastatic breast cancer (MBC), stage 4, with distant metastasis (M1).
- Cancer has spread to distant parts of the body far from the primary site; this is distant metastasis.
- Disease may have developed from earlier stages or presented as de novo stage 4 metastatic breast cancer.
- Primary sites of spread include lung, bone, liver, brain, and distant lymph nodes.
- Invasive breast cancer has grown outside ducts or lobules into surrounding tissue and can spread through lymph or blood.

Plan:
- Continue systemic therapy for metastatic cancer.
- Consider local therapies to treat liver and lung tumors as adjunct to systemic therapy.
- Use expanded biomarker testing to identify targetable features and guide therapy.
- Monitor for distant metastasis progression; assess bone, lung, liver, brain, and distant lymph nodes as clinically indicated.
- Provide patient education and resources: NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Breast Cancer – Metastatic and Invasive available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.
- Maintain contact list for care team; keep information accessible for emergencies and add to phone.
- Encourage use of online patient portal (e.g., MyChart) for appointments and communication with care team.
